| ✅ **Citta-vṛtti-nirodha** | ✅ Citta really takes forms, can be restrained, and is distinct from puruṣa. | ⚠️ Nirodha becomes mere mental quietism, not liberation. |
| ✅ **Kleśa theory** | ✅ Avidyā and its derivatives causally colour cognition, action and rebirth. | ⚠️ Yoga loses its diagnosis of bondage and becomes moral advice only. |
| ✅ **Reflection/asmitā** | ✅ Puruṣa is inactive consciousness; citta is transparent but insentient. | ⚠️ Bondage of a pure puruṣa becomes inexplicable. |
| ✅ **Aṣṭāṅga-yoga** | ✅ Body, conduct, breath, senses and attention condition citta's purity. | ⚠️ Samādhi becomes disconnected from ethics and discipline. |
| ✅ **Samādhi** | ✅ Attention can become progressively object-transparent and finally seedless. | ⚠️ Meditation reduces to trance or concentration without soteriological force. |
| ✅ **Karma-vipāka** | ✅ Actions leave subtle deposits rooted in kleśas and ripen across experience. | ⚠️ Yoga becomes therapeutic psychology rather than a theory of saṃsāra and release. |
| ✅ **Īśvara** | ✅ A special puruṣa untouched by kleśa-karma-vipāka-āśaya is possible and useful for practice. | ⚠️ Yoga collapses toward nirīśvara Sāṃkhya and loses its distinctive devotional aid. |
| ✅ **Kaivalya** | ✅ Puruṣa is ultimately distinct from prakṛti, and prakṛti functions for puruṣa's experience and release. | ⚠️ Isolation becomes unintelligible; Advaitic identity or Buddhist no-self becomes more plausible. |

| ✅ **Buddhist kṣaṇikavāda** | ⚠️ No persisting citta is needed; a stream of momentary cognitions explains experience. | ✅ Yoga invokes citta as a continuing prakṛtic substrate bearing saṃskāras and undergoing pariṇāma. | ⚠️ Momentariness can still explain continuity through causal series without a substance. |
| ✅ **Yogācāra/Vijñānavāda** | ⚠️ External objects are unnecessary; cognition-only explains appearance. | ✅ Kaivalya-pāda realism: objects are not dependent on a single mind, and citta is known by puruṣa. | ⚠️ Shared karmic appearance remains a sophisticated idealist counter. |
| ✅ **Advaita Vedānta** | ⚠️ Why many puruṣas, and why make Īśvara only a special puruṣa rather than the sole reality? | ⚠️ Yoga replies from experience-plurality, Sāṃkhyan realism and the practical need for discriminating each puruṣa from prakṛti. | ⚠️ Advaita presses the unity of consciousness more radically. |
| ✅ **Nyāya** | ⚠️ The self is a substance with adventitious consciousness; why call puruṣa consciousness itself, and why desire cessation of all vṛttis? | ⚠️ Yoga replies that consciousness cannot be an accidental property of the true seer, and nirodha reveals rather than destroys awareness. | ⚠️ Nyāya's commonsense realism about persons and cognition remains attractive. |
| ✅ **Cārvāka** | ⚠️ Puruṣa, karma, rebirth and kaivalya are unverifiable beyond perception. | ⚠️ Yoga replies through disciplined yogi-pratyakṣa, pragmatic transformation and the inadequacy of material pleasure to end suffering. | ⚠️ Public verification remains difficult. |
| ✅ **Mīmāṃsā** | ⚠️ A non-creator Īśvara is otiose; ritual action, not yoga, secures dharma. | ⚠️ Yoga replies that ritual cannot by itself remove avidyā/asmitā, while Īśvara-praṇidhāna directly stabilizes citta. | ⚠️ The traditional Yoga proof of Īśvara's necessity is weaker than Nyāya's creator-God argument. |

| ⚠️ **Husserl's epoché/reduction vs nirodha** | ⚠️ Both suspend the natural attitude toward ordinary experience. | ⚠️ Epoché is methodological and retains the constituting ego; nirodha is soteriological and aims at cessation of the mental stream's binding modifications. |

| Doctrine | Presupposition it rests on | What collapses if the presupposition is denied |
|---|---|---|
| ✅ **Citta-vṛtti-nirodha** | ✅ Citta really takes forms, can be restrained, and is distinct from puruṣa. | ⚠️ Nirodha becomes mere mental quietism, not liberation. |
| ✅ **Kleśa theory** | ✅ Avidyā and its derivatives causally colour cognition, action and rebirth. | ⚠️ Yoga loses its diagnosis of bondage and becomes moral advice only. |
| ✅ **Reflection/asmitā** | ✅ Puruṣa is inactive consciousness; citta is transparent but insentient. | ⚠️ Bondage of a pure puruṣa becomes inexplicable. |
| ✅ **Aṣṭāṅga-yoga** | ✅ Body, conduct, breath, senses and attention condition citta's purity. | ⚠️ Samādhi becomes disconnected from ethics and discipline. |
| ✅ **Samādhi** | ✅ Attention can become progressively object-transparent and finally seedless. | ⚠️ Meditation reduces to trance or concentration without soteriological force. |
| ✅ **Karma-vipāka** | ✅ Actions leave subtle deposits rooted in kleśas and ripen across experience. | ⚠️ Yoga becomes therapeutic psychology rather than a theory of saṃsāra and release. |
| ✅ **Īśvara** | ✅ A special puruṣa untouched by kleśa-karma-vipāka-āśaya is possible and useful for practice. | ⚠️ Yoga collapses toward nirīśvara Sāṃkhya and loses its distinctive devotional aid. |
| ✅ **Kaivalya** | ✅ Puruṣa is ultimately distinct from prakṛti, and prakṛti functions for puruṣa's experience and release. | ⚠️ Isolation becomes unintelligible; Advaitic identity or Buddhist no-self becomes more plausible. |

| Objector | Objection | Yoga's reply | Residual force ⚠️ |
|---|---|---|---|
| ✅ **Buddhist kṣaṇikavāda** | ⚠️ No persisting citta is needed; a stream of momentary cognitions explains experience. | ✅ Yoga invokes citta as a continuing prakṛtic substrate bearing saṃskāras and undergoing pariṇāma. | ⚠️ Momentariness can still explain continuity through causal series without a substance. |
| ✅ **Yogācāra/Vijñānavāda** | ⚠️ External objects are unnecessary; cognition-only explains appearance. | ✅ Kaivalya-pāda realism: objects are not dependent on a single mind, and citta is known by puruṣa. | ⚠️ Shared karmic appearance remains a sophisticated idealist counter. |
| ✅ **Advaita Vedānta** | ⚠️ Why many puruṣas, and why make Īśvara only a special puruṣa rather than the sole reality? | ⚠️ Yoga replies from experience-plurality, Sāṃkhyan realism and the practical need for discriminating each puruṣa from prakṛti. | ⚠️ Advaita presses the unity of consciousness more radically. |
| ✅ **Nyāya** | ⚠️ The self is a substance with adventitious consciousness; why call puruṣa consciousness itself, and why desire cessation of all vṛttis? | ⚠️ Yoga replies that consciousness cannot be an accidental property of the true seer, and nirodha reveals rather than destroys awareness. | ⚠️ Nyāya's commonsense realism about persons and cognition remains attractive. |
| ✅ **Cārvāka** | ⚠️ Puruṣa, karma, rebirth and kaivalya are unverifiable beyond perception. | ⚠️ Yoga replies through disciplined yogi-pratyakṣa, pragmatic transformation and the inadequacy of material pleasure to end suffering. | ⚠️ Public verification remains difficult. |
| ✅ **Mīmāṃsā** | ⚠️ A non-creator Īśvara is otiose; ritual action, not yoga, secures dharma. | ⚠️ Yoga replies that ritual cannot by itself remove avidyā/asmitā, while Īśvara-praṇidhāna directly stabilizes citta. | ⚠️ The traditional Yoga proof of Īśvara's necessity is weaker than Nyāya's creator-God argument. |

| ⚠️ **Husserl's epoché/reduction vs nirodha** | ⚠️ Both suspend the natural attitude toward ordinary experience. | ⚠️ Epoché is methodological and retains the constituting ego; nirodha is soteriological and aims at cessation of the mental stream's binding modifications. |
| ⚠️ **Descartes' cogito vs puruṣa** | ⚠️ Both make consciousness indubitable. | ⚠️ The cogito yields a thinking substance that acts; puruṣa is inactive, non-agentive witness-consciousness. |

| ⚠️ **Freud's unconscious vs saṃskāra/vāsanā** | ⚠️ Both posit latent dispositions shaping conduct. | ⚠️ Saṃskāras are karmically indexed and metaphysically real deposits in a rebirth framework, not merely a psychodynamic hypothesis. |

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: The seventeen sessions below run in teaching order, not in source order. Each session opens with a definition, gives a gateway idea in plain language, shows the concept before it argues it, then supplies the named evidence, the answer-grabbing line, the must-write keywords, a worked answer-paragraph model, the exam route, the traps and a rapid revision strip.
Everything needed for a complete 10-, 15- or 20-mark answer on any routed question is inside this Basic block. The Optional Advanced block near the end of this document is enrichment; no core

Yoga is the one Paper I school whose syllabus clause is a list of five technical nouns — mind-field, mental modification, afflictions, absorption and isolation. The sessions therefore move along the system's own causal spine: first what the mind is, then how it moves, then why its movement binds, then how the binding is dismantled, then what remains when it is gone.
Session | What it settles | Why it comes here

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 1 — WHAT YOGA ACTUALLY IS: RESTRAINT OF MENTAL MODIFICATION AND THE SĀṂKHYA INHERITANCE

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** Yoga, in Patañjali's system, is not a posture practice, not a fitness regime and not a merger of the soul with God. It is the disciplined stopping of the mind's continuous churning, undertaken so that the pure consciousness that was watching all along stops mistaking that churning for itself.

**Technical definition.** Classical Yoga is defined as the restraint of the modifications of the mind-field (**yogaś-citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ**), with the immediate consequence that the seer then abides in its own nature (**tadā draṣṭuḥ svarūpe'vasthānam**). It is described in the tradition as Sāṃkhya-exposition (**sāṃkhya-pravacana**) or theistic Sāṃkhya (**seśvara-sāṃkhya**): it accepts the dualism of conscious witness (**puruṣa**) and primordial material nature (**prakṛti**) and the standard twenty-five principles (**tattva**), and adds a graded practical soteriology together with a special conscious witness, the Lord (**Īśvara**).

Imagine a lamp standing behind a rotating cut-glass drum. The lamp does not move, does not heat up and does not change colour. But the drum spins, and its facets throw moving coloured patterns on the wall. If you watched only the wall you would swear the *lamp* was dancing.

Yoga's whole diagnosis is in that image. The lamp is consciousness; the drum is the mind; the moving patterns are the mind's modifications. The mistake is not that the patterns exist. The mistake is the sentence "I am the pattern." Stop the drum, and the sentence has nothing left to attach to — the lamp is seen simply as the lamp.

This is why the school's opening definition is negative in form and positive in intent. "Restraint" sounds like suppression, but its purpose is disclosure: nothing is created, nothing is destroyed, and one persistent misreading is ended.

decisions.heading: CORE UPSC — THE ARGUMENT IN FULL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **The definition is a definition of a state, not of an activity.** Yoga names the condition in which the mind's modifications have been restrained. Postures, breath-work and ethical vows are *means* that produce that condition; none of them is the definition. This is the single most examinable sentence in the topic, and the one candidates most often replace with a wellness paraphrase.

2. **The second half of the definition supplies the payoff.** Restraint would be pointless quietism if nothing followed from it. Patañjali immediately adds that the seer then abides in its own nature. So restraint is *revelatory*: it removes an overlay, it does not manufacture a new state of the self.

3. **What happens otherwise is stated with equal precision.** When restraint is absent, the seer takes the form of the modifications — that is, consciousness appears to be whatever the mind is currently doing. Bondage in Yoga is therefore a cognitive-phenomenological condition, not a physical chaining of an immaterial thing.

4. **The metaphysics is borrowed, deliberately and openly.** Yoga does not construct a rival cosmology. It accepts the two ultimates and the twenty-five principles and restates only as much of them as its psychology requires. The examiner's implicit test is whether you can distinguish what Yoga *owns* from what it *inherits*.

5. **What Yoga owns is the psychology and the method.** The mind-field, the five modifications, the afflicted/unafflicted division, practice and dispassion, the five afflictions, the moral causation of action, the eight limbs, the absorption taxonomies, combined discipline, the Lord, discriminative knowledge, the cloud-of-dharma absorption and isolation are Yoga's own subject matter.

6. **What is inherited stays labelled as inherited.** Primordial material nature, the conscious witness, the qualities, the twenty-five principles and real transformation are Sāṃkhya's. Yoga uses them; it does not re-prove them, and an answer that spends its length re-proving them has answered the wrong syllabus item.

7. **The addition of a Lord is the school's public signature.** Sāṃkhya in its classical form is Godless. Yoga admits a special conscious witness untouched by affliction, action, fruition and deposit. That single admission is why the tradition calls Yoga *seśvara-sāṃkhya*, and why every comparison question between the two schools ends here.

> **Qualification to keep.** "Theistic Sāṃkhya" is an accurate label but a limited one. Yoga's Lord > is not the material cause of the world, is not presented in the sūtras as a creator in the Nyāya > manner, and does not bestow isolation from outside. The theism is real but bounded, and the > boundary is exactly what the 2025 question rewards.

decisions.heading: HOW TO WRITE THE PARAGRAPH — CLAIM -> NAMED EVIDENCE -> ANALYSIS -> QUALIFICATION

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Claim.** Yoga's originality lies not in what it says exists, but in what it says must be done about it.

**Named evidence.** Its defining aphorism restrains the modifications of the mind-field, its second aphorism restores the seer to its own nature, and its fourth states the alternative — the seer taking the form of the modifications — while its ontology is the inherited Sāṃkhya scheme of many conscious witnesses, one primordial material nature and twenty-five principles.

**Analysis.** Because the two ultimates are already fixed by the inherited scheme, the only work left for Yoga is the work of correction, and correction of a persistent misreading requires training rather than proof. That is precisely why the school's central term is a discipline word, *nirodha*, and why its texts are organised around practice rather than around cosmological derivation.

**Qualification.** The inheritance is not total. Yoga's admission of a Lord marks a genuine doctrinal difference from classical Sāṃkhya, but it is a bounded difference: the Lord functions as an unequalled support for concentration and an obstacle-remover, not as material cause or as the external giver of release.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: - Do **not** define Yoga as union with God. Patañjali defines it as restraint of the mind's modifications; the "union" gloss belongs to devotional and later usage.
- Do **not** write that Yoga rejects Sāṃkhya. It accepts Sāṃkhya's ontology and supplies what Sāṃkhya lacks.
- Do **not** treat posture as the definition or the goal. It is one limb of eight, and the eight limbs are a means to the defined state.

- Definition: restraint of the modifications of the mind-field → seer abides in its own nature.

- Labels: *sāṃkhya-pravacana*, *seśvara-sāṃkhya* against Sāṃkhya's *nirīśvara*.
- One line: *Yoga is Sāṃkhya made trainable, and only secondarily made theistic.*

decisions.heading: SESSION 2 — TEXTUAL IDENTITY: PATAÑJALI, VYĀSA, THE FOUR CHAPTERS AND SOURCE CONTROL

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 2 — TEXTUAL IDENTITY: PATAÑJALI, VYĀSA, THE FOUR CHAPTERS AND SOURCE CONTROL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** Before you can quote Yoga you have to know who said what. The system's base text is a set of short aphorisms; almost everything else that gets attributed to "Yoga" in an exam hall is actually commentary, and mixing the two is the fastest way to lose marks on a source-sensitive question.

**Technical definition.** Classical Yoga is the Pātañjala system set out in the *Yoga-sūtra*, read in the tradition with Vyāsa's *Yoga-bhāṣya* and, later, with Vācaspati Miśra's *Tattvavaiśāradī* and Vijñānabhikṣu's *Yogavārttika*. The *Yoga-sūtra* is organised in four chapters (**pāda**): absorption (**samādhi-pāda**), practice (**sādhana-pāda**), powers (**vibhūti-pāda**) and isolation (**kaivalya-pāda**).

Think of the *Yoga-sūtra* as a set of headings and the commentaries as the paragraphs written under them. The headings are extremely compressed — often three or four words — and were never meant to be read alone. So when a textbook says "Yoga classifies the mind into five levels," the honest sentence is: *the classical commentarial exposition beginning with Vyāsa classifies the mind into five levels, and the classification is standard.*

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: That is not pedantry, and it is not a reason to avoid the fivefold list. It is the difference between a candidate who says "Patañjali lists five mind-levels" — which is false — and a candidate who says "the classical exposition, standard from Vyāsa onward, distributes the mind into five levels" — which is true, and which signals source control to the examiner.

decisions.heading: CORE UPSC — THE ARGUMENT IN FULL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **Patañjali is the traditional systematiser, not the inventor of the practices.** The aphorisms collect, order and define; they do not claim to originate meditation, restraint or dispassion.

2. **Vyāsa's commentary is the classical interpretive baseline.** When later expositors disagree, they disagree within the space Vyāsa opened. For UPSC this means Vyāsa-derived material is safe to use — provided it is named as commentarial when the question is source-sensitive.

3. **The four-chapter division is itself examinable orientation.** A question about the difference between object-supported and objectless absorption is a first-chapter question; a question about afflictions and the eight limbs is a second-chapter question; a question about extraordinary capacities is a third-chapter question; a question about the mind–object realism, discriminative knowledge and isolation is a fourth-chapter question.

4. **The chronology of the text and its commentaries is genuinely disputed.** The layering, dating and even the unity of the sūtra collection are scholarly questions. The correct exam behaviour is to identify the received system confidently and to build nothing on a contested date.

5. **The most frequently mis-sourced item is the five mind-levels.** They are standard in the commentarial exposition and completely usable — including for the 2019 applied question — but they are not a five-item aphorism of Patañjali, and a candidate who claims they are has handed the examiner an error.

6. **The second most frequently mis-sourced item is the four-stage analysis of lower dispassion.** The effort-toward-control, separation, single-residual-desire and mastery sequence is commentarial elaboration; Patañjali's own concise statement of lower dispassion is mastery over thirst for seen and heard-of objects.

7. **The third is the later theoretical proof-set for the Lord.** Arguments from scripture, from maximal degrees of knowledge and power, and from the need for intelligent coordination belong to later Yoga commentators. Patañjali's own grounds are compact and practice-facing.

> **Qualification to keep.** Source control is not scepticism. Nothing in the commentarial layer is > being rejected here; it is being *labelled*. The examiner rewards a candidate who can use the full > tradition and still say which part of it is speaking.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 3 — THE MIND-FIELD (CITTA): CONSTITUTION AND MATERIAL BASIS

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** The mind-field is everything that thinks, decides, remembers, feels and says "I" — taken as one working apparatus rather than as three separate faculties. In Yoga it is made of matter, in a very subtle form, and it is not the self.

**Technical definition.** The mind-field (**citta**) is the internal organ or mind-complex through which cognition, affect, volition and meditative discipline become possible. In Yoga it is not the sensory mind (**manas**) in isolation but the unified internal apparatus comprising determinative intellect (**buddhi**), ego-maker (**ahaṃkāra**) and sensory mind (**manas**). It is a product of primordial material nature and is therefore insentient (**jaḍa**), though as a functioning whole it is predominantly of the lucid quality (**sattva**), which explains its transparency.

Sāṃkhya, being a taxonomist, separates three inner instruments and gives each a job: intellect decides, ego appropriates, mind coordinates. Yoga, being a therapist, mostly stops separating them — because the patient does not experience three faculties. The patient experiences one restless interior.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: That is the entire reason for the term. Bondage does not happen to your intellect while your ego looks on; liberation does not free your sensory mind while your intellect stays trapped. The disease and the cure both concern the whole interior, so Yoga gives the whole interior one name.

decisions.heading: CORE UPSC — THE ARGUMENT IN FULL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **The mind-field is material, in the subtle sense.** It is an evolute of primordial material nature. Nothing about it is intrinsically conscious. This is not a concession Yoga makes reluctantly; it is the premise that makes the whole reflection theory necessary.

2. **It is one apparatus with three functions.** Sāṃkhya's analytic separation is retained as analysis, but Yoga's operative unit is the composite. That is why the school can speak of "restraining the mind-field" as a single project.

3. **Its transparency is explained by the lucid quality.** Because the composite is sattva-predominant, it is subtle and clear enough to take the form of what it attends to and to mirror consciousness. A tamas-heavy instrument could do neither.

4. **The derivation must be stated exactly.** Intellect evolves first from primordial nature; the ego-maker evolves from intellect; the sensory mind evolves from the lucid side of the ego-maker. It is therefore wrong to say that intellect, ego and mind *all* arise directly from sattva-predominant ego-maker. This is a favourite close-option trap.

5. **The mind-field is not the sensory mind of Nyāya.** In Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika the internal sense is atomic, partless and instrumental, and the self is a separate substance to which cognition belongs as a quality. Yoga's mind-field is broad, composite, transformable and karmically loaded.

6. **The mind-field is not the inner instrument of Advaita either.** Advaita's inner instrument operates under beginningless ignorance within a non-dual Brahman framework. Yoga's operates within a plural-witness dualism with no Brahman doctrine at all.

7. **Because bondage runs through the mind-field, so must release.** One cannot free the witness by modifying the witness, which is eternally free and unmodifiable. The only available surface for work is the instrument. That is why Yoga is, in its own self-description, a therapy of attention, habit, impression and misidentification.

> **Qualification to keep.** Saying the mind-field is "insentient" is a technical claim about its > intrinsic nature, not a denial that mental life is luminous. It is luminous — but by reflection, > and the next session is entirely about what that means.

decisions.heading: SESSION 4 — REFLECTION, BORROWED CONSCIOUSNESS AND MISIDENTIFICATION

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 4 — REFLECTION, BORROWED CONSCIOUSNESS AND MISIDENTIFICATION

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** The mind is not conscious, and the self does not act. Yet experience feels like a single conscious actor. Yoga explains the appearance by saying that the mind *mirrors* consciousness — and that the whole of bondage consists in mistaking the mirror-image for the original.

**Technical definition.** Yoga's reflection theory (**pratibimba**; also **chāyā**, shadow-image) holds that the mind-field appears conscious because it stands in proximity to the conscious witness, while the conscious witness appears bound because its light is reflected in the mind-field. The resulting confusion is egoity (**asmitā**) — described as the conflation of the power of the seer with the power of the instrument of seeing (**sva-svāmi-śakti**) — and the relation itself is mere proximity (**sannidhi-mātra**), involving no change in the witness.

Put a clear quartz crystal next to a red flower. The crystal looks red. Nothing has happened to the flower, and nothing chemical has happened to the crystal; the redness is a fact about how a transparent thing behaves next to a coloured one.

Now run the analogy twice, because Yoga does. The mind takes the *colour of objects* — that is cognition. The mind also takes the *light of the witness* — that is the feeling of being someone. Both are borrowings. And the second borrowing is the dangerous one, because when a borrowed light is mistaken for an owned light, the borrower starts saying "I know, I suffer, I want" — and the lender, who never moved, appears to be in trouble.

decisions.heading: CORE UPSC — THE ARGUMENT IN FULL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **The witness cannot literally be affected.** It is unchanging (**apariṇāmin**); therefore it cannot act, suffer, acquire properties or undergo modification. Any theory that lets bondage *really* happen to it has already contradicted the school's definition of it.

2. **The mind cannot be intrinsically luminous.** It is a product of nature and therefore insentient; but its lucid-quality subtlety makes it capable of mirroring. Transparency is a material property; luminosity is not.

3. **Therefore knowledge cannot be modelled on physical contact.** An inactive consciousness cannot collide with an object the way two bodies collide. Yoga's model is proximity-plus-reflection, and it is chosen precisely because contact models are unavailable to it.

4. **Bondage is a double misreading, not one.** The mind's borrowed consciousness is misread as selfhood; the witness's mere witnesshood is misread as agency. Both halves are needed to generate the ordinary sense of being an experiencing doer.

5. **The technical name for this is egoity.** Egoity is the identification of the seer with the instrument of seeing, or of the conscious witness with the intellect. It is an affliction, and Session 10 will place it second in the list of five.

6. **The soteriological consequence is exact.** Since the witness cannot be changed, the task is not to alter the witness but to end the misattribution — by purifying and restraining the instrument in which the misattribution occurs.

7. **The standard image is the crystal near the flower.** A second, exam-friendly image is the magnet and iron filings: mere presence explains movement on the iron's side without any action on the magnet's side. Both images do the same protective work — they let something happen without anything happening to the witness.

8. **The objection is real and must be voiced.** Reflection normally requires some relation between mirror and original. If the two principles are ontologically disjoint, how can the inactive witness be "reflected" at all?

9. **The reply is mere proximity — and its residual force must be conceded.** Yoga answers that all the transformation is on the mind's side; the witness neither acts nor changes. But Advaita and Nyāya can still press the classical difficulty of how two radically different principles combine to yield one experience. The honest verdict names the reply *and* the pressure.

> **Qualification to keep.** "Mere proximity" is best described as naming the relation more precisely > than it explains it. That is the single most useful evaluative sentence in the entire topic, and it > is exactly what a *critically examine* directive is looking for.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Claim.** Yoga's soteriology stands or falls with its reflection theory, because that theory is the only device by which an unchanging witness can be said to be bound at all.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** Minds are not all in the same condition. Yoga sorts them into five working states — scattered, dull, occasionally-focused, one-pointed and fully restrained — and says that only the last two are actually fit for the discipline it teaches.

**Technical definition.** The levels of the mind-field (**citta-bhūmi**) are the five operative conditions of the mind-complex, classified by the dominance of the constituent qualities: scattered (**kṣipta**, active quality dominant), dull (**mūḍha**, inert quality dominant), distracted (**vikṣipta**, mixed with occasional lucidity), one-pointed (**ekāgra**, lucid quality dominant) and restrained (**niruddha**, all modifications arrested).
There is a simple test hidden in this list, and it catches almost every candidate. Ask: is a brilliant research scientist, absorbed in a problem for fourteen hours, in a yogic state?

The intuitive answer is yes — that looks like concentration. The Yoga answer is no. Intensity of attention is not the criterion; *direction and stability of the whole mind* is. A mind can be formidably concentrated and still be outward-turned, ambitious, anxious about results and dependent on its object. That is a mind that flashes lucidity inside a rajas-dominated life. Yoga has a precise name for it, and it is not the name of a yogic state.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **The classification is qualitative, not quantitative.** It records which constituent quality is ruling the mind, and therefore what the mind is *for* at that moment, not how hard it is working.
2. **Scattered is activity without integration.** The active quality supplies motion; desire, worry, ambition and sensory dispersion dominate. This is the ordinary agitated mind.

3. **Dull is obscuration, not peace.** The inert quality supplies torpor, delusion and confusion. It is important to say this explicitly, because a heavy, unmoving mind can be mistaken for a quiet one.

4. **Distracted is the level that flatters itself.** Lucidity flashes; analysis and even brief concentration are available; but the active and inert qualities are not overcome, so the mind cannot remain inwardly collected. This is the condition of many highly capable worldly persons.
5. **One-pointed is the first genuinely yoga-fit level.** The lucid quality predominates sufficiently for meditative absorption to deepen on a chosen support.
6. **Restrained is the culmination, and it is not blankness.** All modifications are arrested. It is the mind-state correlated with the highest absorption and with the approach to isolation.

7. **Only the last two are fully fit.** The first three are pre-yogic or only partially prepared. The transition from distracted to one-pointed is therefore the decisive step of the entire practical path.

8. **The 2019 application is exact and must be justified, not asserted.** A scientist intensely focused on an empirical problem, yet directed outward and attached to worldly ends, is best classified as distracted. A God-realised devotee whose mind is one-pointedly centred on the Lord is one-pointed. A self-realised yogin in whom all modifications are stilled is restrained. The subtlety that earns the marks is the first one: *high intellectual focus does not itself amount to yogic restraint.*

> **Qualification to keep.** This fivefold scheme is standard in Vyāsa's commentarial exposition and > in the tradition that follows him. It is entirely usable — the 2019 paper used it — but it must not > be cited as a five-item aphorism of Patañjali.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** A modification is any shape the mind takes. Yoga says every mental event you can name — a true perception, a mistake, a word-picture with nothing behind it, sleep, a memory — is one of exactly five shapes, and that each shape can either bind you or help free you.

Patañjali classifies all modifications into five kinds: valid cognition (**pramāṇa**), error (**viparyaya**), verbal construction (**vikalpa**), sleep (**nidrā**) and memory (**smṛti**). Each of the five may be afflicted (**kliṣṭa**) or unafflicted (**akliṣṭa**), according to whether it sustains affliction or serves release.
The list looks odd at first, and the oddity is the teaching. Why is *sleep* a mental modification? Why is *true knowledge* on a list of things to be stopped?

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: Because Yoga is not sorting mental events by whether they are good or true. It is sorting them by whether they are *shapes the mind takes*. Sleep is a shape — you wake and report "I slept and knew nothing," which means something was registered. True cognition is a shape — an accurate one, but still a shape. And the problem is never the accuracy of a shape. The problem is that shapes are what the witness keeps mistaking for itself.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **The classification claims to be exhaustive.** Yoga holds that the mind constantly assumes forms corresponding to objects, memories, errors, absences and verbal constructions, and that these five exhaust the field.

2. **Valid cognition is included, and its inclusion is the doctrinal point.** Yoga does not deny valid knowledge; it accepts perception, inference and reliable testimony. But even true cognition is *a modification of the mind*, and modifications are what the witness misidentifies with. Truth does not exempt a mental form from being a mental form.

3. **Error is false knowledge not corresponding to the object as it is.** It covers both perceptual and conceptual misapprehension. Since error reinforces wrong attachment and aversion, it is typically afflicted.

4. **Verbal construction is cognition produced by words alone.** It is not nonsense; it has linguistic intelligibility without an objective referent. Yoga is unusually sensitive here: it sees that language can autonomously generate mental worlds, anxieties, dogmas and imagined identities.

5. **Sleep is a positive modification, not a gap.** The later recollection "I slept and knew nothing" shows that sleep leaves a determinate mental trace; its content is an absence, but the mode is real. Philosophically this matters because it forbids the equation of quiescence with liberation.

6. **Memory is non-loss and re-presentation of prior experience.** It links past impressions to present identity and reaction, and in practical psychology it feeds attachment, trauma, fear and habitual self-narration.

7. **The afflicted/unafflicted division is orthogonal to the fivefold list.** Any of the five can fall on either side. Afflicted modifications are coloured by ignorance and the other afflictions and are therefore bondage-producing; unafflicted ones are purified and redirected toward discrimination, detachment and liberation.

8. **Yoga therefore does not abolish cognition at once.** It first transforms the *quality* of mental life, replacing afflicted modifications with unafflicted ones, and only then lets even those subside once their work is done.
9. **The division qualifies modifications, never afflictions.** Afflictions are inherently afflictive; there is no "unafflicted ignorance". Reversing this is a standard close-option trap.

> **Qualification to keep.** The claim that even valid cognition must finally cease is not a claim > that valid cognition is false or worthless. It is a claim about *category*: what has to stop is > the mind's form-taking, and truth-value is irrelevant to whether something is a form.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 7 — WHY RESTRAINT IS PRESCRIBED: THE ARGUMENT, THE INSTRUMENTS AND YOGIC PERCEPTION

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** This is the "why" half of the definition. Why should a mind that works perfectly well be stopped? Yoga's answer is a five-step argument, and it ends with a claim that restraint reveals rather than destroys.

**Technical definition.** Restraint (**nirodha**) is prescribed because the mind-field takes the form of whatever it attends to, the witness's consciousness is reflected in it, and in ignorance the resulting forms are appropriated as "I know", "I suffer", "I desire", "I remember". The stream of modifications therefore sustains bondage, and its restraint uncovers the already-free nature of the seer. Yoga admits three instruments of valid knowledge — perception (**pratyakṣa**), inference (**anumāna**) and authoritative testimony (**āgama/śabda**) — and treats the perfected insight of the disciplined practitioner as extraordinary yogic perception (**yogi-pratyakṣa**), not as a fourth instrument.

A pool of water reflects the sky. Stir it, and the reflection breaks into a hundred moving fragments; someone reading the fragments would conclude that the sky is chaotic. Let the ripples settle and the same water shows one clear sky.

Nothing was added to the water and nothing was taken from the sky. That is what "restraint is revelatory, not destructive" means. Yoga is not attacking the mind. It is removing the distortion that makes an undistorted thing look distorted.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 8 — SUSTAINED PRACTICE AND DISPASSION (ABHYĀSA AND VAIRĀGYA)

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** Restraint has two handles, and you need both. One is doing the work long enough and steadily enough that it becomes your default; the other is genuinely not wanting the things that pull you off it. Effort without letting-go becomes strain; letting-go without effort becomes drift.

**Technical definition.** Sustained practice (**abhyāsa**) is the effort to remain stable in restraint, and it becomes firmly grounded when cultivated for a long time, without interruption and with devoted seriousness. Dispassion (**vairāgya**) is mastery over thirst; in its lower form (**apara-vairāgya** or **vaśīkāra-vairāgya**) it is the cessation of thirst for seen and scripturally promised objects, and in its higher form (**para-vairāgya**) it is non-thirst even for the constituent qualities of nature, arising from direct discernment of the conscious witness.
Consider two failures that look opposite and are actually the same failure.

The first person meditates rigorously every day and still wants everything — status, comfort, recognition, spiritual attainment. The practice is real; the pull is untouched; every session is a tug-of-war. The second person is genuinely detached — bored of the world, unimpressed by rewards — but never builds a stable practice, so detachment sits as mood rather than as capacity.

Yoga's answer is that restraint is produced by the *pair*, not by either handle alone. And the higher form of dispassion is the surprising one: it lets go not of worldly goods but of the subtle attainments — insight, powers, exalted states — that a successful practitioner is uniquely tempted by.

3. **Practice's function is continuity against old impressions.** Latent impressions push the mind back into habitual forms; only an equally continuous counter-force can hold restraint.

4. **Lower dispassion is defined by what has ceased, not by what is renounced.** Patañjali's own concise definition at *Yoga-sūtra* 1.15 is mastery over thirst for objects that are seen and for objects heard of through scripture. 5. **Higher dispassion is defined by its source.** At *Yoga-sūtra* 1.16 it follows knowledge of the conscious witness and extends renunciation even to the constituent qualities themselves. It is therefore not a stronger version of lower dispassion but a consequence of discernment.

6. **Higher dispassion is what protects an advanced practitioner.** Its specific targets are subtle states, lucid insight and extraordinary powers — the goods that only success makes available. Session 14's warning about powers depends on this.

7. **The four-stage analysis of lower dispassion is commentarial.** Effort toward control, separation of subdued from unsubdued tendencies, withdrawal to a single residual mental desire, and mastery. Use it, and label it.
8. **This pair sits underneath the whole later architecture.** Preparatory discipline, the eight limbs and the absorption ladder are all elaborations of "practise steadily, want less".

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 9 — REAL TRANSFORMATION OF THE MIND-SUBSTRATE (CITTA-PARIṆĀMA)

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** If a person really improves through years of practice, something must persist that is doing the improving. Yoga says the mind genuinely changes — it does not merely appear to change, and it is not replaced moment by moment — and that this persisting-yet-changing mind is what makes a graded path intelligible.

**Technical definition.** Transformation of the mind-field (**citta-pariṇāma**) is Yoga's account of how the mind-complex really changes across practice without losing its continuity as a substrate of nature. The tradition recognises three specifically yogic transformations — of restraint (**nirodha-pariṇāma**), of absorption (**samādhi-pariṇāma**) and of one-pointedness (**ekāgratā-pariṇāma**) — within a general threefold transformation of any substrate: of property (**dharma-pariṇāma**), of temporal character (**lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma**) and of condition (**avasthā-pariṇāma**), all presupposing a persisting substrate (**dharmin**).
A lake can be storm-lashed, then gradually calming, then perfectly still. Three genuinely different states — and one lake throughout.

Now ask the awkward question a Buddhist would ask: why do you need "one lake"? Why not just say there is a series of water-events, each causing the next? Yoga's reply is that its own path presupposes more than succession. Practice accumulates. Impressions are deposited and later retrieved. A practitioner acquires a stable capacity. Those are not descriptions of a series; they are descriptions of something that *carries* what it has undergone.

decisions.heading: CORE UPSC — THE ARGUMENT IN FULL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **Yoga inherits real transformation from Sāṃkhya.** The mind really changes. This is *pariṇāmavāda*, not apparent transformation.

2. **Restraint-transformation explains how cessation becomes a habit.** Impressions of restraint progressively overpower impressions of emergence, so the mind's default shifts from dispersion toward cessation. This is why restraint is not a heroic act repeated forever but a condition that consolidates.
3. **Absorption-transformation explains the movement from many-pointedness to unity.** The multiplicity of contents weakens as one object becomes dominant.

4. **One-pointedness-transformation explains sustained sameness.** Similar cognitive moments arise and subside in an unbroken stream directed at the same object. Notice that even the highest stability is described as a *stream*, not as a frozen state.

5. **The general threefold transformation supplies the metaphysical licence.** Any substrate of nature may change in property, in temporal phase and in condition without ceasing to be the same substrate.

6. **The persisting substrate is doing philosophical work.** Without it, graded progress, impression-deposit, memory and stable acquisition are unintelligible. That is the whole reason Yoga refuses a purely momentary psychology.
7. **The Buddhist objection deserves a full sentence.** A momentarist can argue that a causal series explains continuity without any substance, and that the substrate is an idle postulate.

8. **The reply, and what survives it.** Yoga answers that its own path presupposes accumulation, retrieval and acquisition, which a series of disconnected flashes does not obviously deliver. Both schools admit ceaseless change; the disagreement is whether change requires a bearer. The Buddhist position remains a live alternative, and saying so is what "critically examine" rewards.

9. **The contrast with Advaita runs the other way.** Advaita makes ultimate reality non-transforming and worldly change apparent; Yoga keeps change in mind and nature *real*, and keeps many witnesses. Yoga is therefore squeezed between a momentarism that denies the bearer and an illusionism that denies the change.

> **Qualification to keep.** The persisting mind is a substrate of *nature*, not a self. Saying that > the mind persists is not a back-door reintroduction of a psychological soul; the witness remains > outside every one of these transformations.

**Named evidence.** The tradition names three yogic transformations — restraint-transformation, in which impressions of restraint overpower impressions of emergence; absorption-transformation, in which many-pointedness gives way to unity; and one-pointedness-transformation, in which similar cognitions succeed one another toward the same object — all within the general transformation of property, temporal phase and condition in a persisting substrate.

decisions.heading: SESSION 10 — THE FIVE AFFLICTIONS (KLEŚA) AND THEIR FOUR STATES

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 10 — THE FIVE AFFLICTIONS (KLEŚA) AND THEIR FOUR STATES

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** Below the surface of what you think lies what colours your thinking. Yoga calls these deep colourings afflictions, lists five of them, roots all of them in one, and adds that they operate at four different intensities — including a dormant intensity in which they look absent and are not.

**Technical definition.** The afflictions (**kleśa**) are the causal colourings of mental life that generate binding action and sustain the cycle of rebirth. They are five: ignorance (**avidyā**), egoity (**asmitā**), attachment (**rāga**), aversion (**dveṣa**) and clinging to life (**abhiniveśa**), with ignorance as the root of the rest. They function in four states: dormant (**prasupta**), attenuated (**tanu**), interrupted (**vicchinna**) and fully active (**udāra**).
Two things about this list surprise people.

The first is that ignorance is not defined as not knowing something. It is defined as four specific reversals: taking the non-eternal for the eternal, the impure for the pure, the painful for the pleasant, and the non-self for the self. That is not a gap in information; it is a standing misorientation that structures a whole life.

The second is the last item. Clinging to life is said to be present *even in the learned*. Yoga is explicitly denying that scholarship cures the fear of death, because the fear is carried in impressions rather than in beliefs. That single sentence tells you why the school thinks argument alone cannot liberate — and it is the sentence examiners most reliably reward.

decisions.heading: CORE UPSC — THE ARGUMENT IN FULL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **Afflictions are deeper than thoughts.** They are not items in the stream; they are what colours the stream. This is why they are treated separately from modifications and why a modification can be "afflicted".
2. **Ignorance is the matrix, not merely the first item.** The other four arise within it. An answer that lists five parallel afflictions has missed the structure the question is testing.
3. **Ignorance is defined by four reversals.** Non-eternal as eternal; impure as pure; painful as pleasant; non-self as self. Write all four; each is a separately markable point.

4. **Egoity is the specific confusion of seer with instrument.** More precisely, the identification of the conscious witness with the determinative intellect or the inner organ. It is the affliction that Session 4's reflection theory explains.

5. **Attachment and aversion are memory-driven.** Attachment follows remembered pleasure; aversion follows remembered pain. Together they structure most reactive life — chasing the agreeable, fleeing the disagreeable — and both depend on the memory-modification of Session 6.

6. **Clinging to life is instinctive and carried by impressions.** Its presence "even in the learned" is a doctrinally deliberate claim: it shows that afflictions are not corrected by information, and it is frequently tested.

7. **The four states explain why progress is hard to assess.** A dormant affliction is seed-like; favourable conditions reactivate it. An interrupted affliction merely lost a contest to a stronger tendency — attachment may look absent only because fear is currently louder. Only the attenuated state represents genuine progress, and even it is not destruction.

8. **The therapeutic sequence follows directly from the states.** Gross expressions are weakened by ethical and practical discipline; subtle forms (**sūkṣma**) are burned by meditation; and the seed-state is finally destroyed by discriminative knowledge. This is why mere moral restraint is insufficient.
9. **The afflicted/unafflicted division never applies here.** Afflictions are inherently afflictive. The division qualifies modifications only.

> **Qualification to keep.** Describing ignorance as "existential misorientation" is analytical > phrasing and should be presented as such; the doctrinally exact statement is the four reversals. > Give the reversals first and the interpretation second.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 11 — ACTION, DEPOSIT, FRUITION AND IMPRESSION: THE ENGINE, AND PREPARATORY DISCIPLINE

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** Afflictions do not merely feel bad; they drive actions, and actions leave residues that come back as circumstances. This session is the machinery that turns a psychological problem into a cosmological one — and the first tool Yoga hands you for jamming it.

**Technical definition.** The karmic deposit (**karmāśaya**) is the subtle store of action-traces rooted in the afflictions (**kleśa-mūla**), and fruition (**vipāka**) is its ripening as concrete embodied experience, classically threefold: birth or species-condition (**jāti**), life-span (**āyus**) and experience (**bhoga**). Continuity is carried by impressions (**saṃskāra**) and latent tendencies (**vāsanā**). Action is classified as white (**śukla**), black (**kṛṣṇa**), mixed (**śukla-kṛṣṇa**) and neither-white-nor-black (**aśukla-akṛṣṇa**), the last associated with the practitioner whose action no longer produces ordinary bondage. Preparatory discipline (**kriyā-yoga**) — austerity (**tapas**), self-study (**svādhyāya**) and dedication to the Lord (**Īśvara-praṇidhāna**) — is prescribed to attenuate the afflictions and to cultivate absorption.

Here is the difficulty this session exists to solve. Yoga's diagnosis so far is psychological: afflictions, misidentification, mental forms. But its promise is not psychological — it promises the end of rebirth. How does cleaning up a mind end a cosmic process?

The answer is the chain. Afflictions motivate action; action deposits residue; residue ripens as birth, lifespan and experience; experience generates fresh reaction. Because the *first* link is psychological, work done on the mind is not merely therapeutic — it interrupts a moral-causal engine at its source. That is Yoga's claim to be a soteriology rather than a wellness programme, and it is why the 2021 question can move from "nature of afflictions" straight to "how does removal lead to isolation".

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **The chain must be written as a chain.** Afflictions → action → fruition → deposit → rebirth. Reproducing it in order is worth marks by itself, because it is the structure the 2021 question asks you to dismantle.

2. **The deposit is rooted in the afflictions.** Action binds *because* it is coloured by ignorance, egoity, attachment, aversion and clinging to life. Uncoloured action does not deposit in the same way — which is what the fourth colour of action records.
3. **Fruition is threefold and specific.** Birth or species-condition, life-span, and experience. Naming all three is what distinguishes a doctrinal answer from a vague one.

4. **Impressions and latent tendencies explain continuity.** Repeated cognition and action leave traces; traces dispose future cognition and action. This is the mechanism by which a moral order becomes psychologically self-reinforcing.

5. **The fourfold classification of action grades practitioners, not just acts.** White, black, mixed, and neither-white-nor-black. The last is the yogic category, and it is the doctrinal basis for saying that a liberated practitioner still acts without accumulating bondage.

6. **Preparatory discipline is the first therapy, and its purpose is stated.** Austerity, self-study and dedication to the Lord are prescribed explicitly to attenuate the afflictions and to cultivate absorption. Yoga therefore begins from a deliberate re-education of habit and motive, not from metaphysical argument.

7. **The three components are not interchangeable.** Austerity is disciplined, heat-generating effort; self-study is study and recitation of sacred teaching together with reflective self-examination; dedication to the Lord is surrender of the fruits and of the ego's proprietary claim. Note that the third is also a positive observance in the eight limbs and an independent means to absorption — its triple role is examinable.
8. **The standard objection is about scale.** If release requires exhausting an unsurveyable stock of deposits, release seems indefinitely postponed.

9. **The reply is the burnt seed, with a qualification.** Liberating knowledge and absorption burn the seeds of *future* bondage; only the already-fructifying portion of embodiment continues, like a potter's wheel turning briefly after the potter stops pushing. This is the careful basis for liberation-while-living language in Yoga.

> **Qualification to keep.** The already-fructifying/stored distinction is best introduced with the > later comparative vocabulary flagged as such. The exam-safe formulation is that the momentum of an > already-moving psycho-physical complex may continue after the push of fresh action has stopped.

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **The eight limbs are the mediating architecture of the whole syllabus clause.** The clause names mind-field, modification, afflictions, absorption and isolation; the limbs are the path that connects them. UPSC expects them in any fuller answer even though they are not separately printed.

2. **The restraints are five and universal.** Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, disciplined continence and non-possessiveness. When unrestricted by class or birth, place, time or circumstance, they constitute the universal great vow. This matters philosophically: no exceptional context licenses violence, falsehood or possessiveness for the practitioner.

3. **The observances are five and inward-facing.** Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study and dedication to the Lord. Note the overlap with preparatory discipline: austerity, self-study and dedication appear in both, which is a deliberate structural link and a good line to write.

4. **Posture is a seat, not a display.** Classical posture is the establishment of a steady and comfortable position; its significance is freedom from bodily distraction, since a body at war with itself obstructs one-pointedness.
5. **Breath is the hinge.** Regulation of breathing refines the psycho-physical economy, steadies attention and weakens agitation.
6. **Withdrawal is release, not mutilation.** The senses are freed from compulsive extroversion; it is the transition from embodied preparation to explicitly internal work.

7. **The internal three are graded, not synonymous.** Concentration is effortful fixing; meditation is sustained continuity; absorption is consummated integration in which the object alone shines. Treating them as synonyms is one of the most common errors in this topic.

8. **Combined discipline is a technical composite.** The last three, applied together to one object, constitute the inner technical core of Yoga's contemplative method — the progressive refinement of intentionality until cognition becomes translucent to the structure of its object.
9. **"External" does not mean unimportant.** It means preparatory with respect to the subtler operations of meditative consciousness. The distinction is one of function, not of value.

10. **The nine obstacles and four symptoms are a complete list worth memorising.** Disease, mental stagnation, doubt, carelessness, laziness, sensual non-restraint, false vision, failure to attain a stage, and instability in an attained stage; with suffering, dejection, bodily tremor and disturbed breathing as accompaniments.

11. **The remedies open the door to theism.** Dedication to the Lord is one of the important means of overcoming obstacles, alongside practice of one principle, the four attitudes of friendliness, compassion, gladness and equanimity, breath regulation and suitable supports. This is precisely why questions on absorption so often open into the role of God: Yoga's God is a practice-enabling doctrine, not a creation-first one.

> **Qualification to keep.** The eight limbs are not a syllabus noun. Present them as the practical > architecture that the named nouns require, and keep them proportionate — a ten-mark answer on > absorption should not spend half its length listing postures.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 13 — MEDITATIVE ABSORPTION (SAMĀDHI): THE TWO CLASSIFICATIONS THAT MUST NOT BE CONFLATED

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** Absorption is where attention becomes so unified and transparent that the object alone stands there. Yoga classifies it twice — once by the *factor* accompanying it, once by the *object-level and conceptual overlay* — and the single most punished error in this topic is merging the two lists.

**Technical definition.** Absorption (**samādhi**) is meditative absorption in which the mind-field becomes radically unified and transparent. Object-supported absorption (**samprajñāta**) retains a cognitive support and is therefore called with-seed (**sabīja**, *Yoga-sūtra* 1.46); *Yoga-sūtra* 1.17 characterises it through four accompanying factors — gross deliberation (**vitarka**), subtle reflection (**vicāra**), refined joy (**ānanda**) and bare I-am-ness (**asmitā**). Separately, *Yoga-sūtra* 1.42–1.44 classifies meditative coalescence (**samāpatti**) into **savitarkā/nirvitarkā** for gross objects and **savicārā/nirvicārā** for subtle objects. Supra-cognitive absorption (**asamprajñāta**, *Yoga-sūtra* 1.18) is defined as preceded by the practice of the idea of cessation and as having impression-residue (**saṃskāra-śeṣa**).

You can classify a university course by year-level and by mode of assessment. Both classifications are correct; both describe the same course; and neither is the other. If someone said "the four years of the degree are essay, examination, dissertation and viva", you would recognise the mistake immediately.

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: That is precisely the mistake Yoga candidates make. *Yoga-sūtra* 1.17 classifies object-supported absorption by the factor that accompanies it — deliberation, reflection, joy, I-am-ness. *Yoga-sūtra* 1.42–1.44 classifies coalescence by object-level and by whether conceptual-verbal overlay is present or absent. Writing "the four types of samprajñāta listed by Patañjali are savitarka, nirvitarka, savicāra and nirvicāra" mixes a year-list with an assessment-list, and it is the error the 2020 and 2022 questions are best placed to expose.

decisions.heading: CORE UPSC — THE ARGUMENT IN FULL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **Absorption is not passivity.** It is the highest refinement of attention and the threshold of liberating discernment. Saying so at the start pre-empts the "trance" misreading.

2. **Object-supported absorption keeps a support.** A subtle seed of cognition remains; the mind is profoundly stilled but not free of object-reference. It is called with-seed at *Yoga-sūtra* 1.46 because an object-support is present.

3. **Grid A is the fourfold characterisation of *Yoga-sūtra* 1.17.** Gross deliberation, subtle reflection, refined joy and bare I-am-ness. Two of these need protecting from misreading: the joy is a purified meditative affect attached to the lucid quality, not ordinary pleasure; and the I-am-ness is not the binding affliction of Session 10 but an extremely subtle objectification of the I-sense.

4. **Therefore joy and I-am-ness are not a contested later addition.** They are explicitly present in the sūtra's own fourfold characterisation. What is interpretively delicate is only how later commentators map them onto the coalescence sequence.

5. **Grid B is the coalescence analysis of *Yoga-sūtra* 1.42–1.44.** The sa-/nir- prefix marks the presence or absence of conceptual-verbal overlay, specifically the word-object-knowledge construction; the vitarka/vicāra distinction marks gross versus subtle object.

6. **The sūtra sequence continues past the four coalescences.** *Yoga-sūtra* 1.45 extends the subtle domain up to the undifferentiated condition of nature; 1.46 declares all of these with-seed; 1.47 makes the clarity of subtle coalescence yield inner clarity of the self-field; 1.48 declares the insight there truth-bearing.

7. **Supra-cognitive absorption is defined by two things, not one.** *Yoga-sūtra* 1.18: it is preceded by the practice of the idea of cessation, and it has impression-residue. Both halves must be written, because the second half is what makes the next distinction necessary.

8. **Seedless absorption is a further condition, not a synonym.** *Yoga-sūtra* 1.51: when *that too* — the residual impression left by the preceding stage — is restrained, everything being restrained, absorption is seedless. The safe formula is: *supra-cognitive = modifications stopped, impression-residue remains; seedless = even that residue restrained.*

9. **Two routes are associated with the supra-cognitive movement.** *Yoga-sūtra* 1.19 gives a condition-based route associated with disembodied beings and those merged in primordial nature; *Yoga-sūtra* 1.20 gives the means-based route for other practitioners through faith, energy, mindfulness, absorption and wisdom. Commentators warn that condition-based absorption or nature-mergence need not equal final discriminative isolation. These are routes or bases, not a third main classification.

10. **The relation between impression and restraint explains why calm is not release.** Even when active modifications cease, latent impressions can remain as residual potency — which is exactly the impression-residue of *Yoga-sūtra* 1.18 — so the path must proceed to the restraint of even the subtle seed.

11. **The reply to "is supra-cognitive absorption just sleep?" is structural.** Sleep is itself one of the five modifications; supra-cognitive absorption is the cessation of modifications through discipline. The difference lies in both genesis and value: sleep is natural obscuration, absorption is luminous restraint.

> **Qualification to keep.** The commentarial status of joy and I-am-ness — whether they are > independent coalescences, supervening aspects of the subtle stage, or higher refinements beyond the > four named sa-/nir- coalescences — is genuinely disputed. Report the dispute; do not resolve it.

decisions.heading: SESSION 14 — TRUTH-BEARING INSIGHT, POWERS AND THE CLOUD OF DHARMA

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 14 — TRUTH-BEARING INSIGHT, POWERS AND THE CLOUD OF DHARMA

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** Near the top of the path something remarkable happens: the mind becomes so clear that it grasps its object with a precision ordinary inference and testimony cannot reach. Yoga names it, uses it — and then insists it must also go. Alongside it come extraordinary capacities, which Yoga names, credits and then explicitly calls obstacles.

**Technical definition.** Truth-bearing insight (**ṛtambharā prajñā**) is the special lucidity arising with the clarity of subtle coalescence (**nirvicāra-vaiśāradya**), whose field is a particular object (**viśeṣa-artha**) rather than the universals reached by testimony (**śruta**) and inference (**anumāna**); its impression obstructs other impressions, and when even it ceases, seedless absorption becomes possible. Extraordinary capacities (**siddhi**) are attainments in the outward-turned state but obstacles to absorption (**samādhāv upasargāḥ**, *Yoga-sūtra* 3.37). Cloud-of-dharma absorption (**dharmamegha-samādhi**) is the highest absorption immediately preceding isolation.
There is a sharp internal logic in this session, and it is worth seeing before the details.

Yoga's whole problem is that the witness gets identified with mental forms. Now suppose practice succeeds and produces the most exalted mental form imaginable — an insight of flawless truth, plus the power to know distant things. What is the danger? Exactly the same danger as before, only more seductive. A practitioner who says "I possess extraordinary insight" has re-created egoity at a higher altitude.

So Yoga does something unusual for a mystical tradition: it builds the demotion of its own summit experiences into its doctrine. Truth-bearing insight is a ladder; powers are side-effects and liabilities; and the final absorption is defined by the relinquishing of even the fascination with knowing.

decisions.heading: CORE UPSC — THE ARGUMENT IN FULL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **Truth-bearing insight has a stated source.** It arises with the clarity of subtle coalescence and is linked to the inward clarity that follows the perfection of nirvicārā coalescence.

2. **Its distinguishing feature is its field.** Testimony and inference normally reach universals or general relations; truth-bearing insight has a particular object as its field. Yogic insight therefore reaches the individual in a way ordinary testimony and inference do not.

3. **Its function is competitive, not merely revelatory.** The impression born of truth-bearing insight counteracts ordinary afflicted and dispersive impressions. It is an unafflicted modification cancelling afflicted ones, exactly as Session 6 predicted.

4. **It is not a fourth instrument of knowledge.** Yoga accepts three — perception, inference and authoritative testimony. Truth-bearing insight is best classified as perfected extraordinary yogic perception, an extraordinary refinement of perception rather than a new independent means.
5. **The objection is sharp and should be voiced.** If truth-bearing insight is still a mental modification, how can it help liberation rather than bind?

6. **The reply is the ladder.** Unafflicted modifications can cancel afflicted ones; the truth-bearing impression blocks lower impressions and then itself ceases. It is a ladder that must finally be left behind, and when even its impression ceases, seedless absorption becomes possible.

7. **A caution about comparison must be stated.** Truth-bearing insight should not simply be equated with Aurobindo's knowledge by identity or supermind. The resemblance is thematic only: here it is a purified mental modification that must finally cease; there, supramental knowledge is reinterpreted as a permanent, world-affirming gnosis.

8. **Extraordinary capacities are real in the doctrine and demoted by it.** Higher concentrations may yield such capacities; *Yoga-sūtra* 3.37 states that they are attainments in the outward-turned state but obstacles to absorption when they attract appropriation.

9. **The reason for the demotion is precise.** Powers are not intrinsically liberation and can reactivate egoity, attachment and pride. They belong to the side-effects of combined discipline, not to the essence of isolation.

10. **Cloud-of-dharma absorption is the culmination of non-attachment, not of ambition.** The image is a cloud of dharma raining down the fullness of discriminative knowledge; at this level even fascination with extraordinary knowledge or powers is relinquished, and the practitioner no longer seeks omniscience, attainment or display.

> **Qualification to keep.** Reporting extraordinary capacities is doctrinal exposition, not > empirical endorsement. The exam-safe register is: the classical text owns these claims and > subordinates them to liberation; their independent verification is not part of the philosophical > case.

decisions.heading: HOW TO WRITE THE PARAGRAPH — CLAIM -> NAMED EVIDENCE -> ANALYSIS -> QUALIFICATION

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Claim.** Yoga's treatment of its own summit attainments is deflationary by design, and this is a philosophical strength rather than a piece of pious modesty.

**Named evidence.** Truth-bearing insight arises with the clarity of subtle coalescence and has a particular object as its field, unlike testimony and inference; its impression obstructs other impressions; when even that impression is restrained, absorption becomes seedless; extraordinary capacities are declared attainments in the outward-turned state but obstacles to absorption when appropriated; and cloud-of-dharma absorption is reached only when fascination with knowledge and power has been relinquished.

**Analysis.** Each demotion follows from the school's own diagnosis, since the disease was identification of the witness with mental forms, and an exalted mental form is still a mental form — which is why the summit of the path had to be defined by relinquishment rather than by acquisition, and why higher dispassion rather than further attainment is the operative virtue at that altitude.

**Qualification.** Truth-bearing insight is not admitted as a fourth instrument of knowledge but is classified as perfected extraordinary perception, and its similarity to later integral conceptions of knowledge by identity is thematic only, since in Yoga it must finally cease.

decisions.heading: SESSION 15 — THE LORD (ĪŚVARA): SPECIAL WITNESS, SACRED SYLLABLE AND A LIMITED THEISM

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 15 — THE LORD (ĪŚVARA): SPECIAL WITNESS, SACRED SYLLABLE AND A LIMITED THEISM

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** Yoga believes in God — and then spends most of its doctrine explaining what its God does not do. He does not make the world, does not run it, and does not hand out liberation. What he is, is the one being who was never entangled, and therefore the best possible thing for an entangled mind to concentrate on.

**Technical definition.** The Lord (**Īśvara**) is defined in Yoga as a special conscious witness (**puruṣa-viśeṣa**) untouched by affliction (**kleśa**), action (**karma**), fruition (**vipāka**) and karmic deposit (**āśaya**). In him lies the unsurpassed seed of omniscience; he is the teacher of the ancients, unlimited by time; and he is denoted by the sacred syllable (**praṇava**, OṂ). Dedication to the Lord (**Īśvara-praṇidhāna**) is a positive observance, a component of preparatory discipline and an independent means conducive to absorption and to the removal of obstacles.

Ask what problem a God is being introduced to solve. In Nyāya, God explains why atoms combine and why the moral order is enforced — a cosmological and administrative problem. In Advaita, the personal God is the highest reality under the empirical standpoint — a metaphysical problem.

In Yoga, neither. The problem is practical: minds cannot hold still, obstacles derail practice, and the ego resists surrender. A being who is conscious, unlimited in knowledge, unconditioned by time and demonstrably never entangled is the single most effective object such a mind could take. That is why Yoga's theism is real — the Lord genuinely exists in this system — and bounded: he is instrumental, not constitutive, in liberation.

decisions.heading: CORE UPSC — THE ARGUMENT IN FULL

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: 1. **A separate treatment is necessary even though the syllabus clause does not name God.** Yoga's distinctiveness from Sāṃkhya cannot be explained without the Lord, and UPSC repeatedly asks for his role.
2. **The definition is the doctrinal core.** A special conscious witness untouched by affliction, action, fruition and deposit. Reproducing the fourfold "untouched by" list is worth marks by itself.

3. **He is *special*, not *different in kind*.** He belongs to the category of conscious witness; his distinction is that he was never entangled. This is why Yoga's theism does not disturb the dualist ontology.
4. **Omniscience is stated as an unsurpassed seed.** The gradation of knowledge reaches its limit in him, which is the form the omniscience claim takes in this system.
5. **Timeless teacherhood anchors transmission.** He is the teacher even of the ancients, being unconditioned by time — a claim about authority rather than about creation.

6. **The sacred syllable makes theology practicable.** He is denoted by the sacred syllable, whose repetition with contemplation of its meaning is a canonical practice. This links theology, language, sound and contemplative concentration in one discipline.

7. **He is not a creator in the Nyāya sense.** Primordial nature remains the material basis of worldly evolution; evolution proceeds through the witness-and-nature framework, not through divine creation. Yoga's God therefore differs sharply from the Nyāya God as efficient cause of the world-order.

8. **He is not a devotional saviour.** Devotion is accepted, but the structure of liberation remains impersonal in one crucial sense: it depends on the practitioner's own discriminative knowledge. Later devotional theologies must not be read back into classical Yoga.
9. **His positive roles are five and should be listed.** Object of meditation; aid through dedication; remover of obstacles; perfect model; teacher principle.

10. **This is exactly why Yoga is called theistic Sāṃkhya.** It preserves the Sāṃkhyan dualistic ontology and adds the Lord. The addition is not decorative — it changes the psychological and devotional resources of the path — while leaving the basic dualism intact.

11. **The theism is genuine but limited, and the limits must be stated.** Yoga affirms a real Lord; but he is not material cause, not clearly the Patañjala creator of the cosmos, and not the external giver of isolation.

12. **The classic objection from Godless Sāṃkhya must be answered.** If Sāṃkhya's ontology already explains liberation, why add a Lord? Yoga's answer is pragmatic and soteriological: he offers a unique focus of devotion, removes obstacles and supports absorption. The addition is justified by practical efficacy rather than by an overhaul of metaphysical fundamentals.

13. **And the follow-up objection must be conceded correctly.** If liberation depends on discriminative knowledge, is the Lord redundant? The exact answer is: not redundant, but non-final. He is a privileged aid, not a substitute for discernment.

> **Qualification to keep.** The strongest and safest single sentence on this topic is that the Lord > is *instrumental, not constitutive*, in liberation. It concedes what must be conceded, protects the > theism from inflation, and answers both the Sāṃkhya objection and the redundancy objection at once.

decisions.heading: HOW TO WRITE THE PARAGRAPH — CLAIM -> NAMED EVIDENCE -> ANALYSIS -> QUALIFICATION

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Claim.** Yoga's theism is genuine and bounded, and the boundary is not a weakness of the doctrine but its design.

**Named evidence.** The Lord is defined as a special conscious witness untouched by affliction, action, fruition and deposit; in him lies the unsurpassed seed of omniscience; he is the teacher of the ancients, unconditioned by time; he is denoted by the sacred syllable, whose repetition with contemplation of its meaning is canonical; and dedication to him is at once a positive observance, a component of preparatory discipline and an independent means to absorption.

**Analysis.** Every one of these predicates is practice-facing rather than cosmological, which is why the school can admit a real God without disturbing an ontology in which primordial nature remains the material basis of the world; and it is why the Lord's function is exhaustively described by concentration-support, obstacle-removal, exemplarity and pedagogic authority rather than by creation or judgement.

**Qualification.** Because liberation finally follows discriminative knowledge, the Lord must be described as instrumental rather than constitutive; and the fuller theoretical proof-set from scripture, maximal degrees and cosmic coordination belongs to later commentators and should not be projected back onto the aphorisms.

decisions.heading: SESSION 16 — ISOLATION (KAIVALYA): DISCRIMINATIVE KNOWLEDGE, INVOLUTION AND SELF-ABIDANCE

excluded_non_propositional_fragments.exact_payload: ### SESSION 16 — ISOLATION (KAIVALYA): DISCRIMINATIVE KNOWLEDGE, INVOLUTION AND SELF-ABIDANCE

proposition_mappings.exact_payload: **Plain-language definition.** The end-state. Not union, not merger, not extinction, and not merely the absence of pain — but the witness standing alone, unconfused, with nature's performance for it concluded.

**Technical definition.** Isolation (**kaivalya**) is aloneness or absolute distinctness: the isolation of the conscious witness (**puruṣa**) from primordial material nature (**prakṛti**) and its evolutes. It is reached through discriminative discernment (**viveka-khyāti**), matured by higher dispassion (**para-vairāgya**) and consummated in cloud-of-dharma absorption (**dharmamegha-samādhi**), whereupon the constituent qualities undergo involution (**pratiprasava**) back toward their source and consciousness abides in its own form (**svarūpa-pratiṣṭhā**).
The obvious objection comes first, and every good answer meets it in the opening paragraph: if the witness was always pure, always free and never actually changed, then what exactly is achieved?

Yoga's answer is precise. Nothing is achieved *in* the witness. What ends is a relation — the appropriation of nature's changing forms as "I". Liberation is therefore not the production of a new essence but the ending of a misidentification at the level of experience and bondage. The witness does not become free; it stops being read as bound.

The farmer image makes it concrete. A farmer irrigating a field does not push the water. He breaches the embankment, and water flows by its own nature. Discipline removes obstructions; it does not manufacture the freedom of the witness.
